newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM advisers urge more central bank freedom.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM advisers urge more central bank freedom.

text.p: Advisers to Japan's prime minister on Tuesday proposed giving the nation's central bank more say in forming monetary policy, but stopped short of suggesting it be given the independence which its foreign peers enjoy.

The advisory panel, in a report to Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, proposed curbing some of the government's authority over the Bank of Japan. But in return, the central bank should disclose more about its operations, it said.
"We have now made the first step to securing the Bank of Japan's independence," panel chief Yasuhiko Torii told reporters.
Giving the central bank a freer rein was part of Hashimoto's plan for administrative reforms he had pledged.

The panel urged Hashimoto to revise the 54-year-old Bank of Japan law, which defines the BOJ as a body which has the aim of steering the economy appropriately under the strong influence of the Finance Ministry. The panel said this law was outdated.

To enhance the bank's independence, the government's right to give orders about some of BOJ's operations should be abolished, the report said. It also proposed scrapping the government's authority to fire senior BOJ executives just because their views differed from the government's.
Some economists, however, said the panel's proposals were a bit disappointing.

"It (report) falls short of full independence, clearly. There is obviously reluctance to allow the Bank of Japan to be completely free. That's rather disappointing," said Russell Jones, chief economist at Lehman Brothers Asia in Tokyo.
The report said government officials should not become regular members of the Bank of Japan's policy board, but did not rule out government involvement in forming monetary policy.
Government representatives should be able to attend BOJ board meetings when deemed necessary, and such representatives should be allowed to make proposals, the report said.
Currently, officials from the Ministry of Finance and the Economic Planning Agency are regular members of the BOJ's board, but do not have the right to vote.
The report said the government should be able to put on hold any decision made by the BOJ policy board for a certain length of time if its view differed from that of the BOJ.

"If you look at the examples of other countries where central banks are more independent, central banks have the opportunity to make their case in parliament and in official publications. The government cannot really veto the decision," Jones said.

Although decisions on monetary policy should be left to the BOJ, the government should be involved in dealing with problems in the nation's financial system and cooperating with other countries in times of international financial crises. The government should also be able to make decisions on foreign exchange intervention and state treasury matters, it said.
In return for greater independence, the BOJ should make its decision-making process more transparent to gain credibility and be effective in global financial markets, it said.

One way would be to publicise minutes of board meetings, perhaps via the Internet as in other countries, it said. Or the central bank's overall monetary policies could be explained more thoroughly to the public and to parliament, it said.

The BOJ's policy board should be the sole decision-making body, instead of the BOJ executive members' meetings, which are widely said to be the ones making major money policy decisions while the board endorses them, it said.
